reference.title: Front Plank (male)
reference.listing: Video; data sheet: body part Waist, equipment Body weight, exercise type Strength
reference.note: Reference used only to identify the movement. No GymVisual media is stored here; this rig, model and animation are original.

breathing.pattern: Breathe steadily through the hold: short breaths low into the belly while the brace stays on. Do not hold the breath.
breathing.cadence: About one breath every 3 s during the 9 s hold

prescription.tempo: Hold 10-30 s, build toward 60 s with good form
prescription.holds: Short repeated holds (about 10 s) keep the form crisp for beginners (clinical opinion)
prescription.progression: Longer holds, then a long-lever plank (elbows further forward) or lifting one foot

cues.text: Forearms flat on the mat, elbows under the shoulders, forearms parallel, knees down, toes tucked.
Brace the stomach, squeeze the glutes and lift the knees: one straight line from head to heels.
Push the floor away with the forearms, keep the hips level and breathe steadily.
Lower the knees to the mat under control.

mistakes.fix: Brace the stomach and squeeze the glutes; drop to the knees if the line cannot be held.
Lower the hips until shoulders, hips and ankles line up.

mistakes.mistake: Elbows far in front of or behind the shoulders
mistakes.fix: Stack the elbows directly under the shoulders.
Look at the mat just ahead of the hands; neck long.
Keep short, steady breaths through the brace.

kinematics.norm: Straight line from shoulders through hips to ankles (Schoenfeld 2014 study set-up; clinical opinion for tolerance)
Elbows directly below the shoulders, shoulder width apart, forearms and toes on the floor (Schoenfeld 2014)
About 90 degrees (upper arm vertical, forearm flat) (clinical opinion)
Knees straight in the full plank; the knee-supported version roughly halves abdominal activity (Escamilla 2016)
Set by arm and leg length; about 10-15 degrees for a forearm plank (clinical opinion)
Held 30 s in the EMG study (Schoenfeld 2014); loop shows a 9 s hold

sources.title: Schoenfeld et al. 2014, an electromyographic comparison of a modified version of the plank with a long lever and posterior tilt versus the traditional plank exercise (Sports Biomechanics, doi 10.1080/14763141.2014.942355)
Escamilla et al. 2016, muscle activation among supine, prone and side position exercises with and without a Swiss ball (Sports Health 8(4):372-379)
Cho, Kim and Park 2018, effect of body mass index and sex on muscle activity during trunk exercise (J Exerc Rehabil 14(5):778-782)
Electromyographic analysis of core trunk, hip and thigh muscles during 9 rehabilitation exercises (J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2007; PubMed 18560185)

cautions: Stop if sharp pain, numbness or tingling occurs.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
Low back pain that increases in the plank: shorten the hold or use the knee plank.
High blood pressure: breathe steadily; long breath-held efforts raise blood pressure.
modify: Shoulder discomfort: hands together (forearms in a slight V) or an incline plank with the forearms on a bench.
Elbow discomfort: fold the mat under the forearms.
regressions: Incline plank with the forearms on a bench.
progressions: Long-lever plank (elbows further forward), higher abdominal activity (Schoenfeld 2014).

muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis and the deep abdominals resist the hips sagging. Upper rectus abdominis about 27% MVC in a 30 s forearm plank (Schoenfeld 2014); 34-40% MVIC for upper and lower rectus in a plank on the toes (Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: External oblique was the most active abdominal in the plank: about 50% MVC (Schoenfeld 2014) and 40% MVIC (Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: External oblique was the most active abdominal in the plank: about 50% MVC (Schoenfeld 2014) and 40% MVIC (Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.serratus_r: Holds the shoulder blades flat on the rib cage as the chest pushes away from the floor.
muscleNotes.serratus_l: Holds the shoulder blades flat on the rib cage as the chest pushes away from the floor.
muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_r: Holds the upper arm vertical over the elbow against the forward lean of the body.
muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_l: Holds the upper arm vertical over the elbow against the forward lean of the body.
muscleNotes.pec_r: Helps the anterior deltoid hold the upper arms and keeps the elbows from sliding apart.
muscleNotes.pec_l: Helps the anterior deltoid hold the upper arms and keeps the elbows from sliding apart.
muscleNotes.quads_r: Keep the knees straight; rectus femoris about 20% MVIC on the toes, 7% on the knees (Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.quads_l: Keep the knees straight; rectus femoris about 20% MVIC on the toes, 7% on the knees (Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Rectus femoris and iliopsoas help hold the hips from sagging (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Rectus femoris and iliopsoas help hold the hips from sagging (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.glute_max_r: A light glute squeeze keeps the pelvis neutral (cue from the long-lever plank study, Schoenfeld 2014).
muscleNotes.glute_max_l: A light glute squeeze keeps the pelvis neutral (cue from the long-lever plank study, Schoenfeld 2014).
muscleNotes.lats_r: Latissimus dorsi about 18% MVIC (Escamilla 2016); helps pull the elbows toward the toes.
muscleNotes.lats_l: Latissimus dorsi about 18% MVIC (Escamilla 2016); helps pull the elbows toward the toes.
muscleNotes.triceps_r: Little work in the forearm plank; steadies the elbow (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.triceps_l: Little work in the forearm plank; steadies the elbow (clinical opinion).
